metric_rationale: This metric separates trials by the top-validity cue, which is feature index 0 in this design. Within each side of that top-cue split, it computes the relation between the lower-cue tally advantage for A and actual A choices: mean tally advantage on A-choice trials minus mean tally advantage on B-choice trials, normalized by the tally range of 6. Take The Best predicts this relation is zero on both sides, because the top cue discriminates on every trial and all lower cues are ignored. Tallying predicts a positive relation on both sides, because larger tally advantage for A makes an A choice more likely. The two side-wise values are averaged, and a minimum response-class size of 12 avoids unstable undefined estimates while keeping the metric tight within subjects. Under Take The Best the expected value is near zero; under Tallying it is clearly positive.

This metric is a crossover contrast using the design's matched pairs. It first computes, for every trial, which option Take The Best would select by scanning cues in descending validity order. It then subtracts the observed A-choice rate on trials where TTB selects B from the A-choice rate on trials where TTB selects A. Under Tallying, the two TTB-predicted trial sets are balanced in signed tally margin d: each has one pair at d=+2, one at d=-2, one at d=+1, one at d=-1, and two at d=0. Since Tallying predicts p(A)=sigmoid(beta*d) after noise, the positive-d and negative-d contributions cancel exactly, so the expected value of this metric is zero for every beta and epsilon, leaving only binomial sampling variance. Under TTB, every trial in the TTB-selects-A set has A-choice rate p and every trial in the TTB-selects-B set has A-choice rate 1-p, so the metric equals 2*sigmoid(beta)-1 shrunk by 1-epsilon. Each subject contributes 48 trials to each side, producing a large mean separation with low per-subject variance.

The metric averages three signed contrasts between trial types that have the same tally difference (0, +1, and -1) but opposite validity configuration. Within each matched pair, Tallying must assign identical choice probabilities regardless of beta or epsilon, so its expected signed contrast is exactly zero. NWA instead predicts a large positive contrast in each pair because a high-validity advantage makes that option less likely. Averaging three independent contrasts, each estimated from 12 repeated presentations, yields an expected NWA score near 0.90 with small per-subject variance.

On all 2-vs-2 zero-net-tally pairs Tallying predicts p(A)=0.50 exactly for every beta and epsilon, because the softmax over equal tallies is uniform and the lapse mixture remains uniform. NWA instead predicts a graded ordering: trials where A wins the two highest-validity features get strongly negative scores and low p(A), while their mirror-image trials get strongly positive scores and high p(A). The metric contrasts empirical A-choice rates on the two high-NWA mirror pairs against the two low-NWA mirror pairs: mean choose A given diff in {(-1,-1,1,1),(-1,1,-1,1)} minus mean choose A given diff in {(1,1,-1,-1),(1,-1,1,-1)}. Its expected value is 0 under Tallying and approximately 0.62 under NWA at the stated parameters. It deliberately ignores the 3-vs-1 trials, whose Tallying predictions vary with beta and would add Tallying-side variance.

This metric estimates the conflict-gating contrast that separates VWEA-CG from NWA in this design. For each subject it identifies the four repeated trial types and computes p(choose A). It then compares the extremeness of choices, measured as absolute distance from chance 0.5, between the two aligned pairs and the two tally-conflict pairs. NWA predicts the two positive-U pairs and the two negative-U pairs have identical validity-weighted scores, so aligned and conflict pairs are equally extreme and this contrast is approximately zero. VWEA-CG predicts that high tally-conflict pairs are strongly attenuated toward chance, while matched aligned pairs remain decisive. Taking absolute distance from chance makes the contrast positive for both negative-valence and positive-valence VWEA-CG subjects, reducing between-subject variance while preserving the large theoretical separation. Averaging per subject gives a stable point estimate and keeps the metric well defined on single-subject slices.

Trials are ordered by a validity-weighted conflict score computed from the squared communicated validities. The first four low-score pair types and the last two high-score pair types are used. NWA predicts that the probability of choosing A decreases monotonically as this score increases, so p(A in low-score trials) - p(A in high-score trials) should be large and positive. VWEA-CG predicts that conflict attenuation pushes choices on the largest-score trials back toward chance, so the same contrast should be near zero or slightly negative. Each subject sees all pair types repeatedly, so the contrast is stable at the single-subject level and has low binomial variance.

Compute the validity-weighted difference D = sum_j v_j^gamma (A_j - B_j) with the design validities and central gamma 2.25. Mark each trial as sign-consistent when the subject chose B for D > 0 or A for D < 0, then regress this indicator on the absolute value of D. NWA predicts that sign-consistent choice probability rises steeply with |D|, giving a large positive slope. CNVW-tau passes D through the saturating transform D/(tau+abs(D)), which compresses all nonzero |D| values in this design into a flat plateau, so its within-sign slope remains near zero even though the overall sign-consistency level can be high. Using all 96 trials and the paired positive/negative D mirrors removes the sign main effect and pools information efficiently, keeping the between-subject variance small relative to the between-theory contrast.

The metric measures a within-subject psychometric gain: how much more often choices follow the negative-validity prediction when validity-weighted evidence is strong (abs(D) >= 0.90) than when it is weak (abs(D) <= 0.25). D is computed as sum over features of v^2.25 * (A - B) using the instructed validities. NWA uses a single logistic in D, so its consistency rises sharply from weak to strong evidence, giving an expected raw high-minus-low contrast near 0.37. CNVW-tau instead passes D through D / (tau + abs(D)), a strongly saturating bounded transform, which compresses this gain to an expected raw contrast near 0.15. Taking the absolute value at the subject level makes the metric insensitive to the small minority of positive-sign subjects allowed by CNVW-tau, while preserving the large NWA gain. The contrast uses only repeated within-subject weak-evidence and extreme-evidence trials, so binomial noise is small and the between-theory gap is expected to be large relative to between-subject variance.
